title: Krishna Slays the Crane-Demon Bakasura
story:
The days in Vrindavan had fallen into a pattern: the boys led the calves out in the morning, the sun climbed, and the river ran. Then one day they came to the pasture and found it was not empty.

Something stood there, huge and still. As the boys drew near, they saw what it was — a crane, but no crane of the river or the reeds. It was enormous, tall as a thing that had grown out of the ground, and it stood planted on the grass, watching. The boys stopped where they were, the calves bunched behind them and lowed, and for a long moment nothing on the riverbank moved. Then they understood: it was not a bird at all, but a demon in the shape of a crane. Baka, the old verses call him — a friend of Kamsa, the king of Mathura who had sent one demon after another against the cowherds' child.

They had no time to warn one another. The great bird struck, and in a single motion it opened its long beak and swallowed Krishna whole.

The boys cried out. Balarama stood frozen, and the rest of them could only stare at the place where their friend had been standing, and at the throat of the monstrous bird. In that black moment they thought they had lost him. A demon had taken the child who never seemed afraid of anything, and the riverbank felt suddenly enormous and empty.

But inside the crane, Krishna was no morsel to be scorched and digested. He was the fire itself. He blazed at the very root of the creature's palate, and the heat climbed, and the great bird that had gulped him down to be rid of him found it could not hold him for another moment. Its beak gaped wide and flung him out onto the grass — whole, unharmed, not even singed. The boys' cries turned, in an instant, to something else.

Then the demon came at him, enraged and beating its wings, and Krishna did not wait for it to reach him. He took hold of the bird by the two halves of its long beak, one in each hand, and tore it apart the way a child splits a stalk of grass. The crane that had swallowed him fell broken to the ground, and did not move again.

The boys could hardly believe what their eyes had seen. They ran to Krishna as though he had come back to them from far away. The old verses catch the moment in a single image: it was as if their very breath, which had left their bodies when he vanished down that throat, now returned to them. And from the sky above, the dwellers of heaven, who had watched it all, let fall a shower of flowers — blossoms drifting slowly down over the children, over the fallen demon, over the quiet water of the Yamuna. The herd grazed on as before, and the boys sat down in the grass to catch their breath, and after a while they led the calves home in the long, level light of evening.
reflection: Bakasura swallows Krishna and discovers, too late, that he has taken in what he cannot contain. But the story's real center is the image of the boys' breath returning — what the demon meant to take, Krishna gives back.
content_note: Krishna is swallowed by a demon crane and tears it apart; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
next_story_tease: The demons were not finished: Aghasura, brother of the slain Putana and Bakasura, was already nursing his revenge.
hero_scene: Krishna gripping the two halves of the giant crane's beak, one in each hand, tearing it apart as flower petals drift down from heaven and the cowherd boys watch in wonder on the bank of the Yamuna.
